distinguishing_feature: GERD is dominated by heartburn and acid regurgitation; functional dyspepsia presents with epigastric pain/fullness without a clear acid-reflux pattern and normal endoscopy.
Distinguished only by endoscopic findings: esophagitis (visible mucosal breaks) is present in the latter, absent in the former, despite similar symptoms.
Presence of overt bleeding (hematemesis, melena, or endoscopic evidence of bleeding esophagitis) distinguishes the bleeding variant.

Sideropenic (Plummer-Vinson) dysphagia is gradual, painless, associated with iron-deficiency anemia and an esophageal web; post-stroke dysphagia is sudden-onset and accompanied by other neurological deficits.
Both present with acute neurogenic dysphagia; distinguished by neuroimaging showing ischemic infarction versus intracerebral hemorrhage as the underlying cause.
Functional diarrhea is loose stools without associated abdominal pain meeting IBS criteria; IBS-D includes recurrent abdominal pain linked to altered bowel habit.
Slow transit constipation is confirmed by prolonged colonic transit time on testing; unspecified constipation has not yet been characterized by such studies.

Outlet dysfunction constipation involves difficulty with rectal evacuation (straining, incomplete emptying) due to pelvic floor dysfunction, typically confirmed by anorectal manometry or defecography, rather than slow colonic transit.
Drug-induced constipation has a clear temporal relationship to starting a constipating medication (e.g. opioids, iron, anticholinergics) and often improves on discontinuation.
Chronic idiopathic constipation is a broader diagnosis of exclusion; slow transit constipation is a specific subtype confirmed by transit studies.

Crohn's disease can affect any part of the GI tract with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; ulcerative colitis is continuous, limited to the colon/rectum, and mucosal only — distinguished on endoscopy and biopsy.
Proctitis is limited to the rectum on endoscopy; pancolitis involves inflammation extending through the entire colon — extent on colonoscopy is the distinguishing feature.
Rectosigmoiditis is limited to rectum and sigmoid colon; left-sided colitis extends further, up to the splenic flexure — again distinguished by colonoscopic extent.
A rectal polyp is a discrete mucosal growth seen on endoscopy; rectal prolapse is protrusion of the full rectal wall through the anus, visible on physical exam, especially with straining.
An abscess is an acute, painful, localized collection of pus; a fistula is a chronic abnormal tract (often a sequela of a prior abscess) with intermittent drainage rather than acute severe pain.
Distinguished by fistula complexity/anatomy on exam or imaging: a 'simple' fistula has a single, low tract not involving significant sphincter muscle, versus a complex/unspecified presentation.
Swallowed maternal blood (from delivery or a cracked nipple) is confirmed with an Apt-Downey test showing adult hemoglobin; true neonatal GI bleeding shows fetal hemoglobin and needs its own work-up.
Bilious (green/yellow) vomiting suggests intestinal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater and is a surgical emergency; non-bilious vomiting has a broader, usually less urgent differential.

Late vomiting of pregnancy refers to onset in later pregnancy (after the typical first-trimester window), which itself should prompt considering other causes; unspecified vomiting of pregnancy has no documented timing.
